observed_change: Hierarchical territorial administrations linked royal appointees, local offices, taxation, recruitment, and crisis response.
evidence: Royal country lists, classical appointments, and administrative reconstruction
limits: Satrap and satrapy are imprecise Greek labels for offices and units at different levels.

observed_change: Alexander preserved most eastern administrative structures, retaining some officials and replacing others with trusted appointees.
evidence: Appointments preserved in Alexander narratives and reconstructed against late Achaemenid administration
limits: Continuity of territorial machinery did not preserve Achaemenid sovereignty or an unchanged bureaucracy.

observed_change: The Babylon settlement distributed satrapies and left several Asian and Indian rulers in place.
evidence: Diodorus 18.3 lists assignments and explicitly says remaining Asian satrapies were not disturbed
limits: A later Greek narrative records a political settlement, not a complete administrative register.

observed_change: Seleucid kings governed large eastern provinces as Upper Satrapies while adding co-rule, cities, Greek institutions, and a new dynasty.
evidence: Scholarly synthesis of Seleucid political geography and administration
limits: Rough territorial correspondence is not proof of unchanged borders, staffing, fiscal practice, or local administration.

observed_change: Regional formations were connected to senior command, supply, and campaign plans without becoming one uniform military system.
evidence: Herodotus, Xenophon, Arrian, and the regional Persepolis administrative archive
limits: The window is not a continuous force series and accepts no ancient headline army total.

observed_change: Iranian commanders and cavalry entered Macedonian command structures; at Opis, Persian and Median units received Macedonian unit names.
evidence: Later Arrian narrative of appointments and the Opis settlement
limits: This was a contested late-reign experiment, not proof of a stable fusion policy or a successor-wide institution.

observed_change: The successor settlement reallocated provinces and commands, but the evidence does not establish one inherited mixed imperial army.
limits: Absence of a shared continuation in this comparison is not evidence that Iranian formations or practices disappeared.

observed_change: Imperial Aramaic supplied a portable chancellery language and script across distant provincial administrations.
limits: Use varied by region; this does not imply one language displaced local written traditions.

observed_change: Provincial scribal styles diverged; Aramao-Iranian inscriptions in the east continued an administrative writing tradition under new states.
evidence: Epigraphic comparison of provincial styles and Aśokan-era inscriptions
limits: Script descent is not institutional identity, and the surviving inscriptions are unevenly distributed.

observed_change: Aramaic ductus and syntax on early Persis coins developed toward Middle Persian Pahlavi spellings.
evidence: Dated coin legends and paleographic sequence
limits: Coin legends are a narrow medium and do not reconstruct a complete chancery.

observed_change: Middle Persian, Parthian, Sogdian, and Chorasmian scripts developed from regional Aramaic traditions with different rules.
limits: The long range joins distinct regional lineages; it is not one standardized script or continuous archive.

thread_title: Local Persian rule recombined old forms
observed_change: The title frataraka is documented for district heads below the satrap in Achaemenid Egypt.
limits: An Egyptian administrative title does not by itself establish the later office held by Persis dynasts.

thread_title: Local Persian rule recombined old forms
observed_change: Persis dynasts probably began as Seleucid representatives, used Aramaic legends, and stressed Achaemenid ties in coin imagery.
limits: The title's reading and political status are debated; the dynasts did not initially claim empire-wide kingship.

thread_title: Local Persian rule recombined old forms
observed_change: Arsacid rulers left Persian dynasts in office with minting rights; later local rulers used the title king.
evidence: Numismatic sequence and regional political synthesis
limits: Local coinage does not measure autonomy, territorial reach, or continuous descent from Achaemenid officeholders.

thread_title: King of Kings was revived not inherited continuously
observed_change: Achaemenid royal inscriptions presented the ruler as great king and king of kings over multiple countries.
limits: Royal titulature expresses a claim and hierarchy, not measured control over every named land.

thread_title: King of Kings was revived not inherited continuously
observed_change: This comparison does not plot a continuous Achaemenid title-line through the Macedonian and Seleucid dynasties.
evidence: Contrast between Achaemenid, Hellenistic, and later Arsacid titulature
limits: A plotted gap is a warning against direct inheritance, not a claim that Achaemenid royal memory vanished.

thread_title: King of Kings was revived not inherited continuously
observed_change: Mithradates I introduced King of Kings late in his reign; from Mithradates II it was often used with new Arsacid genealogical claims and imagery.
evidence: Numismatic titulature and scholarly reconstruction of Parthian kingship
limits: The date and first use remain debated; revival was part of a new Arsacid ideology, not restored Achaemenid government.

thread_title: King of Kings was revived not inherited continuously
observed_change: Ardashir and Shapur made King of Kings of Iran and non-Iran a Sasanian imperial title tied to a new geography and religious-political vocabulary.
evidence: Royal inscriptions, coin legends, and kingship synthesis
limits: The Sasanian title was a redesign with new terms and claims; shared wording does not prove an unchanged institution.
